extracted.intended_audience: Authors submitting manuscripts to peer-reviewed journals (academic researchers awaiting editorial decisions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on what the Editorial Manager status 'Decision in Process' means, how long it typically takes, when and how to inquire, and productive actions to take while waiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral meaning of 'Decision in Process'
rubrics_metrics.description: The status indicates the editorial team is finalizing a decision; it does not automatically mean rejection or acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the status as neutral. It signals movement from review/evaluation phases to decision formulation by Associate Editor and final authority, but predicts nothing definitive about outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish scenario: post-peer-review vs editorial evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: This status typically appears either after external peer review completes (editor synthesizing reviewer feedback) or after an internal editorial evaluation without external review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check prior statuses and timeline: if the manuscript was 'Under Review' for weeks, this likely follows peer review; if 'Decision in Process' appears within days and you never saw 'Under Review', it may indicate editorial (desk) decision. The two scenarios have different implications (post-review often suggests potential for revision; pre-review often leans to desk rejection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical duration ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Most manuscripts remain in 'Decision in Process' for 1–4 weeks, though timelines vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fast track: 1–2 weeks (clear consensus). Standard: 2–3 weeks. Extended: 3–4 weeks (conflicts, board consultation). Unusually long: 5+ weeks — consider polite inquiry after 4 weeks. Use these ranges to set expectations but expect exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeline factors that affect duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple factors influence how long 'Decision in Process' lasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key factors: reviewer consensus (adds 0–3 days if minimal), conflicting reviews (add 1–2 weeks), editor availability (3–10 days), holiday periods (2–4 weeks), editorial board review (3–7 days). Also consider manuscript complexity, clarity of reviews, and strategic fit with journal schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial workflow steps behind the status
rubrics_metrics.description: Three main internal steps: Associate Editor synthesizes inputs; recommendation proceeds to final authority (Editor-in-Chief or committee); formal decision entry and communication preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that synthesis and hierarchical review take time and that administrative tasks (system entry, letter customization, formatting reviewer comments) can delay visible communication even after the decision is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the status does NOT indicate
rubrics_metrics.description: The status does not definitively indicate rejection, desk rejection, or prompt timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming outcome or timeline from the status alone. Timing context and previous statuses matter more. Different journals/systems label stages differently; the same label can mean different internal steps across publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2-3-4 week rule for inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Guideline for when authors should contact the journal about prolonged 'Decision in Process' status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Week 1–2: wait. Week 3–4: consider a gentle inquiry. Week 5+: follow up (appropriate). If the journal's stated timeline is exceeded, or there are time-sensitive circumstances, inquire earlier. Use provided email templates and send to the editorial office.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to make a polite status inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct brief, professional, and understanding emails to the editorial office when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use templates like: Subject: Status Inquiry - Manuscript [ID Number]; briefly state dates and that you understand review takes time; request confirmation the submission is progressing normally. Email editorial office (not individual editors unless appropriate). Expect a few days for reply; avoid repeated follow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: What NOT to do when following up
rubrics_metrics.description: Behaviors that harm professionalism or annoy editors when inquiring about status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not send multiple emails days apart, use aggressive language, fabricate deadlines, CC multiple people, or threaten withdrawal unless you mean it. Avoid unsolicited attempts to influence the decision—decisions are based on merit, reviews, and fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red flags suggesting system or administrative issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns that likely indicate problems rather than normal deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Decision in Process' appears then disappears without communication; status persists >3 months; no substantive reply after inquiries; evidence handling editor left (or other staff changes). In these cases escalate to publisher support phrased neutrally (e.g., concern manuscript may be lost).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to escalate beyond the editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for contacting publisher support or editorial office higher-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Escalate after two polite emails spaced ~2 weeks apart with no substantive response, if timeline exceeds the journal's promised timeframe by ~50%+, or if you have evidence of system issues. Escalate via publisher’s editorial support rather than blaming individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productive actions to take while waiting
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended activities authors should pursue during the 'Decision in Process' period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare for possible revision (review manuscript, refresh literature, identify potential analyses), identify alternative journals strategically (not just prestige-based), and advance other research projects. Being prepared shortens response time if revision is requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and avoid common myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent misconceptions about what the status implies and how to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myths to avoid: quick status=reject, long status=accept, contacting editor will influence outcome, status changes predict decisions. Recognize these as unreliable and avoid behaviors based on such assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding publisher- and field-specific variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Status labels and update timing vary across manuscript management systems and disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-compare experiences with colleagues using different systems/publishers. Learn your field and target journal norms (ask colleagues or check journal guidelines) for more accurate expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible outcomes and appropriate next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcomes that can follow 'Decision in Process' and recommended author responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcomes include: accept/accept with minor revisions (follow revision instructions promptly), major revision/revise-and-resubmit (respond thoroughly to reviewer comments), rejection with encouragement to resubmit (assess whether resubmission is worthwhile), rejection with recommendation to submit elsewhere (choose alternatives), outright rejection (learn and move on). Prepare responses based on the type of decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative delays vs. substantive deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish delays due to administrative processing from active deliberation or undecided outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administratively, preparing letters, formatting reviewer comments, and system entry can delay communication even after a decision is made; this explains why 'Decision in Process' can persist. Do not conflate administrative lag with the nature of the editorial decision.
